The Data Recipient agrees to process the Data only for the following purposes agreed with the HSCIC: 
Objective for processing: 
The primary aim of the National Joint Registry for England, Wales, and Northern Ireland (NJR) is to monitor and improve patient safety and outcomes.  The NJR forms part of the National Clinical Audit and Patient Outcomes Programme (NCAPOP) which is delivered by the Healthcare Quality Improvement Partnership (HQIP) under contract to the Department of Health.  The work of the NJR is overseen by an Expert Advisory Group which is responsible to NHS England.  HQIP sub-contract to Northgate Public Services for the provision of data services and the University of Bristol for statistical and analysis services.  As the owner of the data, HQIP are the data controller and Northgate Public Services and the University of Bristol are both data processors.  The University of Bristol, however, only have access to pseudonymised, sensitive data.
One of the means by which that aim is achieved is through the creation of an annual dataset which consists of NJR, HES, Patient Episode Database Wales (PEDW), and PROMs (NHS England programme) data.  This dataset is used primarily for the production of the NJR’s Annual Report, its associated analyses, and in some reporting services provided to stakeholders.  NJR stakeholders include patients, clinicians, Trust and hospital management, the medical device industry, and regulatory bodies. The majority of this research and analyses is based on NJR data. The data will be used solely for the purposes stated, although the outputs may be used for other purposes when made available publicly (as stated). 
By linking to HES, PROMs and ONS Mortality data, the NJR is able to enhance the quality and type of analyses that it undertakes.  For example, the NJR uses two endpoints to determine outcomes:  death and revision.  
HES data required for:
The linkage to HES data also enables the NJR to improve the type and quality of the analyses that it can undertake without having to collect the data itself.  Such linkage may be length of stay linked to outcomes or co-morbidities linked to outcomes.  The priorities for NJR analyses and research are set by the NJR’s Research Committee and Editorial Board, both of which report to the NJR Steering Committee
Patient reported outcome measures  (PROMs) data required for:
By linking to PROMs, outcomes analyses will improve as poor performance will be detected even if the primary joint replacement procedure has not been revised.  Linkage to PROMs and analysis at the record level enables the NJR to monitor the performance of hospitals, surgeons, and individual implants.
Death Data required for:
The NJR is required to publish 90 day mortality rates in Annual Clinical Reports to Trusts, the NJR’s Annual Report and as part of the national consultant outcomes programme.  This latter information is also re-published by NHS Choices.  Mortality analyses has also been included in a number of papers, most notably a paper which examined the link between death from certain types of cancer to metal on metal hip replacements.  In order to undertake this reporting and analyses, the NJR relies on both revisions and death as endpoints, and the date of death is required to calculate the time to death from the date of the procedure.  The date of death is provided to the University of Bristol but is not included in any reports.  The cause of death is also required so that the mortality rates can be statistically risk-adjusted to ensure that comparisons of mortality rates at a surgeon and hospital level are safe. 

Processing activities: 
The HES and PROMS data is linked to the NJR data at the episode /NJR procedure level, using a number of fields, including:  ProviderCode (procode3 and proccode5), local patient identifier, NHS Number, epistart and epiend.
Identifiers are necessary to link the HES ONS and PROMs data to NJR data.  Although the primary linkage is a patients NHS number, other data items are used to ensure that the linkage is accurate.  Northgate has developed and refined the linkage algorithm since 2006.   As well as aiding the linkage activity, some fields are also used for analyses:  a surgeon code, for example, enables the monitoring of compliance with the NJR (the NJR is a mandatory data collection) at a surgeon level.
Pseudonymised and sensitive data is then made available to the University of Bristol who are contracted by HQIP to prepare data for analyses and research and to provide statistical support and analyses to the NJR. 
Northgate retain the data sent by the HSCIC for the duration of the agreement and it is then destroyed.
The data is transferred to the University of Bristol using a dedicated, Northgate Secure FTP site.  Once in possession of the pseudonymised and sensitive linked data set, the University of Bristol prepare it for the analyses.  This will result in the creation of a number of smaller, record level datasets that are analysed using Stata or SPSS, dependent upon the statistician.  Where required, the aggregated outputs of some analyses, especially outlier analysis, will be passed to Northgate for publication in online services.
All data provided to the University of Bristol are pseudonymised & sensitive and with Date of Death but no other patient identifiers are included.  The outputs of all analyses are aggregated for use by stakeholders.

Specific outputs expected, including target date(s): 
The outputs from the use of the data will vary each year, dependent upon the research and analysis priorities agreed by the NJR Steering Committee.  The main vehicle for publication is the NJR’s Annual Report which is published annually in September.  In addition to the Annual Report, a Patient’s Guide to the Annual Report is also published and made available in both hard and electronic copy.
Additional analyses are undertaken throughout the year and these are published either in the NJR website or in relevant medical journals. To date those professional journals have included The Lancet, the British Medical Journal, and the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery.  The outcomes are also made available through the NJR’s various online services (NJR Management Feedback, aimed at Trust and clinical management; NJR Supplier Feedback, enabling device manufacturers to monitor the performance of their own devices), the Clinical Outcomes Programme, and NHS Choices.  
As described above, ONS data is required for death date and cause of death.  The date of death is linked to the date of procedure at the record level in order to determine mortality rates.    A patient who has died with a viable implant also has to be removed from any outlier analysis.  The cause of death is also required to ensure that the mortality rates can be risk adjusted to ensure a like to like comparison.  Outlier analysis includes surgeons, hospitals, and implants and takes place twice a year.  The outcomes of the analysis are published in NJR Clinician Feedback (a secure online service that enables surgeons to monitor their clinical practice and compare it, anonymously, with that of their colleagues at a local, regional and national level) and in NJR Management Feedback, another secure online service which enables Trust Management to monitor performance at a hospital and surgeon level.  Where outlier performance is suspected, separate manual, notification processes are enacted before the data is made public.  This is to ensure that local audit can take place in order to confirm outlier status.
Ninety day mortality rates are also published as part of the Clinical Outcomes Programme, and ONS data is essential for this indicator.  The outcomes are also shared with, and published by, NHS Choices.  All outputs are based on aggregated data.
Details of the services provided and the many ways in which the data is used are provided on the NJR website:  www.njrcentre.org.uk.  The data is not used for commercial purposes.

Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care, including target date(s): 
The NJR is an ongoing clinical audit which started to collect data in April 2003.  It has no specific target date for the delivery of benefits:  these are provided on an ongoing basis.
In order to achieve its goals, the NJR requires data, including linked data, to monitor the performance of surgeons, hospitals, and implants in order to improve both patient safety and patient outcomes. By making its data as widely available as possible to its stakeholders, the NJR has become a model for clinical audits.
The NJR was responsible for identifying the high failure rate of the DePuy ASR Hip Resurfacing system which led to the company withdrawing it from sale, not only in the UK, but worldwide.  Many international regulators, including the US, without a national registry, look to the NJR for such intelligence.  In addition to improving patient outcomes and safety, the cost to the NHS of unnecessary revision operations and follow up treatments will have been significantly reduced.   As a direct result of the ASR failure, the Beyond Compliance Programme was established and which relies on the NJR for support.  The programme is voluntary and goes beyond the normal regulatory requirements for introducing a product to the UK market: there are currently over 30 products going through the process which seeks to introduce devices in a more controlled and trialled fashion.
The NJR also highlighted the high failure rates of the use of large head, stemmed metal on metal replacement and was involved in research, using linked data, of the potential damaging side effect of metal on metal articulation.  Both the use of large head, stemmed metal on metal and metal on metal articulation in hip joint replacement has practically ceased in the UK.  An article published in the British Medical Journal, based on local data, purported to show that metal on metal led to an increased chance or dying of cancer.  Using  a national sample of linked NJR data, the NJR, in a paper published in The Lancet, was able to prove that this was not actually the case.  For further detail on papers produced by the NJR please go to http://www.njrcentre.org.uk/njrcentre/Research/NJRIndepthstudies/tabid/315/Default.aspx.
As part of its remit, the NJR continues to identify suspected outlier performance in surgeons, hospitals and with implants, and works with the regulatory authorities, hospital management, and individuals to address suspected poor performance.  The NJR has clearly demonstrated that it can improve patient safety and outcomes and that its outputs have a demonstrable effect on clinical practice.
As highlighted above, the NJR provides a number of services and information to its many stakeholders which include patients, clinicians, management, industry, service commissioners, regulators, and researchers.
